metaDescription: Six leaf vacuums at or under $200, including cordless 40V mulchers and a Greenworks 48V, compared on bag size, impeller design and battery packs.
expertTake: The Greenworks 48V is the pick for a cordless vacuum from a brand with real parts support and batteries that work in other tools. The MZK 40V is the value choice when you want a big claimed airflow and a large bag. A buyer with a small yard can stay with a corded machine and save the money.
introParagraphs: Moving up from the corded machines, the main thing a larger budget buys is freedom from the cord. Cordless leaf vacuums carry a heavy battery and bag, so balance and weight matter as much as airflow.
The questions to ask are how big the pack is, how the impeller handles twigs and whether the bag is practical. Prices move, and the $200 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: Greenworks 48V 520 CFM Cordless Leaf Vacuum 2 x 4.0Ah
products.description:
The Greenworks runs on two 24V packs working in series to make 48V, so the tool gets higher-voltage performance while each pack stays smaller and lighter. Higher voltage lets the motor draw less current for the same power, which keeps it cooler and holds output as the packs drain. The listing claims 520 CFM and 240 MPH, a believable pair for a 48V brushless machine.

It blows, vacuums and mulches, and the two 4.0Ah packs give a workable session on a typical suburban lot. Compared with the MZK at 700 CFM, the airflow claim is lower, but the platform and parts support are stronger. The 24V packs are part of a wider family, so you may find they work in other tools.

Ownership is easier with a mainstream brand: replacement packs, bags and impellers are stocked, and the warranty is a known quantity. Empty the bag at half full, keep twigs out of the intake and clear the impeller with the packs removed. Store the packs indoors, partly charged, and expect the motor to outlast the first set. It is the sensible cordless buy for most homeowners. One practical detail is charging: with two packs you need both topped up before a session, so keep the charger on a shelf indoors and start charging the evening before.
products.bestFor: Cordless cleanup with reliable brand support.
pros: Higher-voltage setup from two compact packs
Established brand with parts and warranty
Two 4.0Ah packs and charger in the kit
cons: Lower airflow claim than the MZK
Two packs add weight on the handle

products.name: MZK 40V Brushless Leaf Vacuum Mulcher 700 CFM
products.description:
The MZK claims 700 CFM from a brushless 40V motor and ships with a 40 liter bag. A bag that size means fewer stops to empty it, which is the annoyance that dominates real-world leaf vacuum use. The listing also highlights an anti-jam design, suggesting the impeller path is shaped to clear matted material.

The 700 CFM claim is higher than the Greenworks's 520, but a maker number at the nozzle is not directly comparable, and an obscure brand carries more uncertainty on measurement. Treat it as a strong but unproven claim.

Support is the question. Check whether replacement packs and impellers are sold, and keep the receipt. Store the battery cool and partly charged. It is for buyers who want maximum capacity and bag size at a lower cost tier. Because a 40 liter bag is large, a full one can weigh enough to pull the tool sideways, so empty it when it is about two thirds full. Leaf dust from shredded material is fine, so wear a mask and eye protection.
products.bestFor: Large bag capacity and high claimed airflow.
pros: Large 40 liter bag reduces emptying stops
Highest airflow claim among the cordless picks
cons: Claimed airflow is a maker figure

products.name: Heywork 40V Brushless Cordless Leaf Vacuum Mulcher
products.description:
The Heywork pairs a brushless 40V motor with four speed settings. Four levels let you vacuum at a gentler rate to save battery on loose leaves and step up for denser material. That control is a real advantage in a heavy cordless tool where battery is the limiting factor.

Like the MZK, it is a newer brand, so support is a question. In design terms it is similar, so the choice may come down to bag size and which listing includes the pack you want.

Store the battery cool, empty the bag regularly and keep twigs out of the intake. It suits a mid-sized yard where control matters. Think about the sound too: a brushless motor at a lower speed setting is noticeably quieter, which neighbors will notice on early weekend mornings. Using the lowest setting that still moves the leaves also stretches the battery.
products.bestFor: Mixed leaf and clippings cleanup with speed control.
pros: Blow, vacuum and mulch in one

products.name: MAXLANDER 3-in-1 Brushless Cordless Leaf Vacuum
products.description:
The MAXLANDER is a cordless 3-in-1 with a brushless motor and a collection bag, described as an upgraded version of an earlier machine. Brushless power reduces heat and wear compared with brushed designs.

The listing gives fewer hard numbers than the Greenworks or MZK, which makes comparison harder. Treat it as a capable tool with less documented performance.

Check pack inclusion before buying, since a bare tool needs a battery. Store the pack indoors. If you buy it, confirm that the listing includes the battery and charger rather than a bare tool, because the pack is the costliest part of a cordless machine. Keep the box and receipt in case of early failure.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want brushless cordless power.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER Backpack Blower Vacuum Mulcher 250 MPH
products.description:
This BLACK+DECKER puts the motor and bag on your back, which moves weight to your shoulders and hips rather than your wrists. It is a corded 3-in-1 with a zipper-free bag, designed for easier emptying, and claims 250 MPH air speed.

Backpack designs make long sessions more comfortable than hand-held ones, but the cord still limits reach and the unit adds weight overall.

It is the choice if you collect a lot of leaves near an outlet and want less arm fatigue. Remember the cord is part of the weight: a long heavy extension cord drags behind you and can snag on shrubs, so plan a path around beds and keep the plug at your back. Backpack straps should be adjusted so the load rides on your hips.
products.bestFor: Long corded sessions with less arm fatigue.
pros: Backpack style spreads weight to the shoulders
cons: Heavy to wear on a hot day

products.name: WORX Trivac WG509 Corded 3-in-1 Leaf Vacuum
products.description:
The Trivac is included as the corded benchmark: it claims 350 CFM and 210 MPH, and its cost advantage over the cordless machines is real. If your yard sits near an outlet, it does the job without batteries to buy or replace.

It is lighter than the cordless machines because it carries no battery, and its mulching impeller is a proven design. The tradeoff is the cord and a lower airflow claim than the MZK.

Choose it if you want cheap, dependable leaf collection within cord range. Keep a spare bag or two on hand, because bags are the part that wears first from abrasion and mold. Dry the bag fully before folding it away, or it will smell by spring.
products.bestFor: Cord-range yards that want the lowest ownership cost.
pros: No battery to buy or replace
cons: Lower airflow claim than the MZK

buyingCriteria.explanation: Cordless vacuums carry packs and a full bag, so total weight climbs quickly. The Greenworks 48V splits power across two 24V packs. A heavy tool tires you before the battery runs out, so balance matters. Weigh the tool with a full bag in mind, not just empty, since a loaded bag can add a good deal to the carry load. Finally, check that the replacement bag and impeller are listed for sale before you commit.

The MZK ships with a 40 liter bag. A big bag cuts stops but adds weight when full. Look for a bag that opens fully for emptying. A bag that is too small turns a ten minute job into a thirty minute one, so favor capacity if your yard drops a lot of leaves.

The mulching impeller shreds leaves and can jam on twigs. Anti-jam designs like the MZK's help, but no impeller loves sticks. Pre-clear branches. Never feed sticks or acorn clusters in, because even an anti-jam shape cannot save a plastic impeller from hard debris.

The Greenworks 48V claims 520 CFM and the MZK 40V 700 CFM. Higher voltage supports sustained power, but maker claims differ in method. When two tools claim similar CFM, the one from a brand with a clear parts catalog is the safer long-term buy.

The BLACK+DECKER backpack spreads weight to your shoulders, while handhelds load your wrists. Choose backpack for long sessions. If you vacuum for more than twenty minutes at a time, a backpack layout is usually kinder to your shoulders and wrists.

The WORX Trivac needs a cord but weighs less and has no pack to age. Cordless saves tangles but adds battery cost and weight. Count total cost: a cord and extension are cheap, while a second battery pack can cost half the tool.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power platform
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared voltage class and battery arrangement. The Greenworks 48V scored highest. Unstated pack details lowered scores. This is why a mainstream brand often outranks a newer one with a bigger claimed number.

howWeEvaluated.title: Collection design
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at bag size and emptying design. The MZK's 40 liter bag and the BLACK+DECKER's zipper-free bag scored well. A bag that is awkward to empty costs more time than a slightly weaker motor ever will.

howWeEvaluated.title: Claim realism
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared airflow claims to voltage and motor type. A 700 CFM claim from an obscure brand was treated cautiously. Where numbers were missing we marked the tool down for transparency, not for performance.

howWeEvaluated.title: Support
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored brands with accessible parts and warranty. Greenworks, WORX and BLACK+DECKER led. A reliable warranty and available parts counted as much as the headline airflow claim.

howWeEvaluated.title: Handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at weight distribution and backpack design from the listings. Backpack designs scored higher for long sessions than handhelds with similar power.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A durable impeller and a large bag. Shredded leaves compost faster and fill fewer bags.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The MZK and Greenworks are the best cordless fits, and the WORX Trivac the corded one.

cards.text: You want a metal impeller and a larger pack for acreage. Higher-end 40V tools sit above this cap.

maintenance.why: A full bag cuts suction and adds weight. Keep packs off a cold concrete floor in winter, which slows charging and shortens life.
Wet leaves wrap the impeller. Remove the pack first. Use compressed air on the motor vents rather than water.
Lithium cells age faster when stored full or empty.

faq.q: Is cordless strong enough for leaves?
faq.a: On a typical lot, a 40V or 48V tool is. Wet leaves and acreage still favor corded or gas. Airflow claims also differ in how they are measured, so rely on platform and motor type when in doubt.

faq.q: Why does the Greenworks need two packs?
faq.a: It combines two 24V packs in series for 48V, which supports higher power with smaller packs. Use a dry, ventilated space for charging to reduce wear.
Yes for fewer stops, but a full bag is heavy. Empty it at half full. Dry leaves flow much better and shred more cleanly than damp ones.
They clog the impeller. Let them dry first. It is worth buying a spare bag at the same time as the machine.
Expect fade after several seasons. Store them cool and partly charged.
